The Mozote Massacre, Morazan, El Salvador 1982

The Mozote Massacre took place in and around the village of El Mozote, El Salvador, on December 11, 1981, when the Salvadoran Army killed more than 800 civilians during the Salvadoran Civil War.

Prior to the massacre, unlike many villages in the area, El Mozote had a reputation for neutrality. While many of its neighbors were largely Roman Catholic, and sympathetic to the guerrillas, El Mozote was largely Evangelical Protestant. The village had sold guerrillas some supplies but was also a place where the guerrillas had learned not to look for recruits

On the afternoon of December 10, 1981, units of the Salvadoran army's Atlacatl Battalion arrived at the village after a clash with guerrillas in the vicinity. It was the first counter-insurgency unit of its kind in the Salvadoran armed forces and was trained by US military advisors to eliminate the rebel presence.

The soldiers reassembled the village in the square and proceeded to interrogate, torture, and execute the men. Then they began taking the women and older girls and machinegunning them after raping them.They then killed the children at first by slitting their throats, then by hanging them. After killing the entire population, the soldiers set fire to the buildings.

In December 2011, the El Salvador government apologized for the massacre.

There's actually something interesting about this quote. It's obviously completely true that it seems like if you talk to the average voter they're going to be poorly informed on at least some relevant topics, yet if you look at polls of the masses on most topics we actually tend to get it right - very right. This isn't just politics. Look at things like the old game show "Who Wants to be a Millionaire." One of the one-time use abilities contestants had was to poll the audience on the question. And even for incredibly esoteric stuff that there's no way the average audience member would know, the answer would tend to come out almost invariably in favor of the right answer.

This is a well known phenomena, 'The Wisdom of the Masses.' Another example is the classic problem of guessing how many peas in a jar, the weight of an ox, and so on. Even though most people will be pretty far off - if you average the answer you tend to get it extremely near exactly right. However, this effect tends to disappear if people are allowed to talk to each other. The problem being that 'experts' aren't necessarily experts, but the people able to convince other people they are. CNN's technical and security expert comes to mind: "This hacker known as 4chan, he may have been a system administrator..." Charisma over competence.

The issues are brought up and people are free to do their own research and come to their own conclusion.
